transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well… I suppose I’m here because my wife thinks I’m getting too caught up in something, and maybe I am, but it doesn’t feel like I’m inventing it. It’s been going on for about a year now. There are these late meetings she has at work, and then small changes in the way her work messages come through, or the timing of them, or little wording things—nothing huge if you look at one piece by itself, I know that. She keeps saying it’s just normal office stuff, schedules shifting, people being vague, that sort of thing.

But when you see it all together, it lines up too neatly. Too precisely. Like there’s a private signal in it, almost like she’s trying to communicate something without saying it directly. And I’ve tried to explain that to her, but she just says I’m reading into it. Maybe that’s why I’m here—to have someone actually listen to the pattern instead of dismissing it as coincidence.
Do you believe your wife is definitely sending hidden messages through those work communications?

I mean… “definitely” is a strong word, and I know how it sounds when I say it out loud. But yes, I do think there’s something there. My wife keeps saying the late meetings and the little shifts in her work messages are just normal office things—people changing schedules, rushed wording, whatever—and if it were one or two times, I might accept that.

But this has been going on for about a year, and it’s the way all the pieces line up. The timing, the wording, when she does and doesn’t answer, certain little changes that seem too precise to be accidental. It feels like there’s a private signal in it, like she’s trying to tell me something without actually saying it directly. I’m not saying it’s written in plain English, obviously, but it feels meant for me to notice.
Do you believe your wife is being unfaithful to you?

Unfaithful… I don’t know if I can say that in a simple yes-or-no way. That’s part of what’s so frustrating, because if I say “yes,” then it sounds like I’m accusing her outright based on nothing, and if I say “no,” then I’m ignoring what’s been right in front of me.

What I do believe is that she’s trying to tell me something without saying it directly. The late meetings, the way her work messages come in, the little changes in wording or timing — she says it’s all normal office stuff, and maybe each piece by itself could be explained that way. But for the past year, when I put it together, it lines up too precisely to feel accidental.

So… is it an affair? Maybe. I can’t prove that. But it feels like there’s some private signal in it, something meant for me to notice, like she knows something is going on and is leaving clues instead of just telling me plainly.
Is it possible that you might be mistaken about these messages having a hidden meaning?

I mean… yes, I suppose it’s possible in the abstract. I’m not trying to say I’m incapable of being wrong. I know people can misread things, especially when they’re worried or when something matters to them. And I know my wife says it’s just normal office stuff — late meetings, messages coming through differently, people at work being rushed or vague, small changes in wording or timing.

But when I actually look at what’s happened over the past year, it doesn’t feel like a simple misunderstanding. It’s the way the pieces keep lining up. One late meeting, fine. One odd message, fine. But over and over, with the timing and the wording and the way certain things appear right when they do… it feels too precise to be accidental.

So yes, could I be mistaken? I guess technically, yes. But it doesn’t feel that way to me. It feels like there’s a private signal in it, like she’s trying to tell me something she won’t just say directly. That’s what I can’t get past.
Have you heard voices or other sounds that other people couldn’t hear?

No… I don’t think so. Not voices, anyway. I’m not hearing someone talking when nobody’s there, if that’s what you mean.

I mean, sometimes I’ll notice ordinary sounds more than other people seem to — like a phone notification, or a door closing, or someone moving around in another room — but I wouldn’t say it’s something other people couldn’t hear. It’s more that I pay attention to things, maybe too much sometimes. But no, I haven’t had voices speaking to me or anything like that.
Have you had the feeling that your thoughts were being controlled or interfered with by someone or something outside yourself?

No, I don’t think so. I mean, I’ve felt preoccupied, definitely — like my mind keeps circling back to certain things and I can’t easily let them go — but that feels like me thinking, not like someone putting thoughts into my head or controlling them.

I’ve never had the sense that some outside force or person was reaching in and changing my thoughts, if that’s what you mean. Sometimes I wish I could stop thinking about things so much, but it still feels like my own mind doing it.
Apart from your wife, do you generally find it hard to trust other people?

Generally? No, I don’t think so. I mean, I’m not someone who walks around assuming everyone is out to get me or that people are lying to me all the time.

I can be cautious with people, I suppose. I think most adults are, to some extent. At work, for example, I don’t automatically tell everyone everything personal, and I pay attention to whether someone is reliable or not. But I wouldn’t say I generally find it hard to trust people across the board.

With most people, I take them more or less as they come. If someone gives me a reason to trust them, I trust them. If they give me a reason not to, then I don’t. So… no, apart from my wife and the situation with her, I wouldn’t describe myself as especially distrustful of other people.
Did this belief about your wife begin very suddenly?

No, not like overnight. It wasn’t one of those things where I woke up one morning and suddenly thought, “This is happening.” It’s been more gradual than that, I think.

It’s been going on for about a year now — roughly since my wife started working outside the home again. That’s when I began noticing things more, and the thoughts sort of built up from there. At first it was just little things, and I tried to tell myself I was overthinking it, but over time it became harder to ignore.

So… no, I wouldn’t say it began suddenly. It developed over time, over this past year.
Before this started, had you developed any medical or neurological illness?

No, not that I’m aware of. I mean, I haven’t had anything like that happen beforehand — no major illness that I can point to and say, “That changed things.”

I suppose everyone has ordinary aches and stresses and that sort of thing, but in terms of a medical or neurological problem before all this started, nothing comes to mind. If there was something subtle, I wouldn’t know, but no doctor told me anything like that, and I didn’t notice some big health change right before it began.
Have other people told you that your speech or behavior has seemed disorganized or hard to follow?

No, I don’t think so. Nobody has said anything like, “You’re not making sense,” or that they can’t follow what I’m saying.

I mean, sometimes if I’m upset or I’m trying to explain something complicated, I might go into a lot of detail — probably too much detail, honestly — and people might get impatient or say I’m overexplaining. But that’s different from being disorganized, I think. At work, for example, I’m expected to communicate clearly enough, and I haven’t had anyone tell me my speech or behavior seems strange in that way.

So as far as I know, no. I haven’t noticed that, and other people haven’t really told me that either.
Other than the situation with your wife, do you have any other beliefs that other people say are strange or hard to believe?

No… I don’t think so. Not outside of this, really.

I mean, I know people might say the thing with my wife sounds hard to believe, but to me it isn’t some random belief I picked up. It’s more that, over the past year, certain things have lined up too precisely. Like the late meetings, or these small changes in her work messages — the wording, the timing, things that she says are just normal office stuff. And maybe to someone else that sounds like I’m reading into it, but when it happens again and again, it starts to feel like there’s a pattern there.

Almost like… not exactly a code, but a private signal, something meant to tell me what she won’t actually say directly. That’s the part other people don’t seem to understand. They’ll say, “It’s just work,” or “People have late meetings,” and yes, I know that in general. I’m not saying late meetings don’t exist. But these particular things, the way they happen together, it feels too exact to be accidental.

But other than that situation with her, no, I can’t think of other beliefs people would call strange. It’s really centered on that.
Have you seen things that other people could not see?

No, I don’t think so. I mean… not in the sense of seeing a person standing there that nobody else can see, or objects moving, or anything like that.

Sometimes I notice things other people don’t seem to notice, but that’s more about paying attention, I think — like small details or patterns. But visually, like actually seeing something that isn’t there, no. I haven’t had that kind of experience.

There are times when I’ll double-check something, like if I think I saw a message notification or something out of the corner of my eye, but then it’s just the usual kind of mistake people make when they’re tired or distracted. Nothing where I’d say, “I saw something and everyone else says it wasn’t there.” So… no, I don’t think so.
During the past year, have you had a period when your mood was unusually high or irritable?

Unusually high? No, I don’t think so. Not high like overly happy or energized in a way people would notice, if that’s what you mean.

I’ve definitely been irritable at times, but I think that’s been more in reaction to stress and arguments, not like a whole separate period where my mood changed and stayed that way for no reason. I can get frustrated, sure, especially when I feel like something isn’t being taken seriously, but I wouldn’t describe it as unusually irritable overall.

So… I guess my answer is no, not that I’ve noticed.
Over the past year, have you found that you care much less about things or have less motivation to do everyday activities than you used to?

No, not really. I mean, I wouldn’t say I’ve stopped caring about things in general or that I can’t get myself to do normal activities.

I still show up for my teaching sections, and I keep up with the data analysis I’m supposed to be doing. I ride my bike pretty regularly, too — not every single day, but enough that it’s still part of my routine. And I still meet friends for chess, which I wouldn’t do if I’d completely lost interest in things. I actually still enjoy that, especially because it’s structured, you know, there’s something clear to focus on.

The main place where things get disrupted is at home, when my wife and I get stuck arguing about her work schedule and what it really means. That can take over an evening, and then I might not feel like doing much afterward. But it’s not like I’ve lost motivation across the board. It’s more that this one situation keeps pulling energy and attention away from everything else.
Over the past year, has your ability to function at work or in your daily life gotten markedly worse?

Markedly worse? I don’t think I’d put it that strongly. I mean, I’m still functioning. I still show up for my teaching sections, and I’m not missing them or just disappearing or anything. I keep up with the data analysis I’m supposed to be doing, maybe not always with the same mental space I’d like, but it gets done.

And day-to-day, I still have routines. I ride my bike, I meet friends for chess, I do those things. So it’s not like my life has collapsed or I can’t manage basic responsibilities.

Where it does get worse — or where it causes the most trouble — is at home. My wife and I can get stuck arguing about her work schedule and what it really means, and then that can eat up a lot of time and energy. It can make the evening feel like it’s been taken over. So yes, it causes problems, but I wouldn’t say my overall ability to work or get through daily life has gotten markedly worse. It’s more contained than that, mostly around the arguments with her.
Do you think your wife is communicating with you through secret codes hidden in ordinary work messages?

I wouldn’t put it exactly like “secret codes,” because that makes it sound… I don’t know, like something from a movie. But yes, I do think there are things in her work messages that mean more than she admits.

She’ll say it’s just normal office scheduling — a late meeting, a small change in wording, a time shifted by half an hour, some ordinary little phrase — but over the past year, those things have lined up too precisely to feel accidental. It’s not one message by itself. If it were one message, fine, I could ignore it. It’s the pattern. The timing, the way the wording changes, when the meetings appear, when they get moved. It feels like there’s a private signal in there, like she’s trying to communicate something indirectly instead of just saying it to me plainly.

And when I ask her, she says I’m reading too much into it, but that doesn’t really answer why it keeps happening in these exact ways. So… yes, I think there’s meaning hidden in ordinary work messages. I don’t know if I’d call it a code, but it feels intentional.
Before these beliefs started, did you begin using any drugs or start any new medication?

No, not that I can think of. I mean, I wasn’t suddenly using drugs or anything like that before this started, and I don’t remember starting some new medication around then.

I’m trying to think if there was anything even incidental — like a cold medicine or something I took once or twice — but nothing that stands out as a real change. My routine was basically the same. If you mean recreational drugs, no. And if you mean a prescription that began right before all this, I don’t think so.
Have you ever heard your wife’s voice speaking to you when she was not actually there?

No, I don’t think so. I mean, I’ve replayed conversations with her in my head, obviously — especially after an argument, where I can almost hear the tone she used or remember exactly how she said something — but that’s memory, not her actually speaking when she isn’t there.

I haven’t had a situation where I’m sitting alone and suddenly hear her voice talking to me from another room or anything like that. If I hear something, there’s usually a real explanation, like the TV, or someone outside, or just me thinking about what she said earlier. So no, not in the sense that you mean.
Have ordinary events or objects ever suddenly seemed to carry a special message meant specifically for you?

Yes… I think that’s probably the closest way to describe it. Not every object or every little thing, but ordinary things like her work messages, meeting times, the wording she uses, small changes that other people would probably say are meaningless. To me they don’t feel random.

She’ll say a late meeting is just a late meeting, or that a phrase in a message is just how people at her office talk, or that a time shifting by half an hour doesn’t mean anything. And if it happened once, I’d agree. I’m not saying one calendar change proves anything. But over the past year, these things have lined up in a way that feels too precise. Like the timing and the wording are arranged to carry something extra.

It feels like there’s a message meant for me in it — not always clear, not like someone handing me a note and saying exactly what they mean — more like a private signal. Like she’s trying to tell me something indirectly, something she won’t just say out loud if I ask her. And when I do ask, she tells me I’m reading into it, but that doesn’t really make the pattern go away. So yes, ordinary things have seemed to carry a special meaning for me, especially with her work messages and those late meetings.

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether there are any other unusual or hard-to-believe fixed beliefs, which directly relates to delusions.

patient.answer:
No… I don’t think so. Not outside of this, really.

I mean, I know people might say the thing with my wife sounds hard to believe, but to me it isn’t some random belief I picked up. It’s more that, over the past year, certain things have lined up too precisely. Like the late meetings, or these small changes in her work messages — the wording, the timing, things that she says are just normal office stuff. And maybe to someone else that sounds like I’m reading into it, but when it happens again and again, it starts to feel like there’s a pattern there.

Almost like… not exactly a code, but a private signal, something meant to tell me what she won’t actually say directly. That’s the part other people don’t seem to understand. They’ll say, “It’s just work,” or “People have late meetings,” and yes, I know that in general. I’m not saying late meetings don’t exist. But these particular things, the way they happen together, it feels too exact to be accidental.

But other than that situation with her, no, I can’t think of other beliefs people would call strange. It’s really centered on that.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there are prominent hallucinations in another sensory modality, which would support schizophrenia or a psychotic disorder due to a medical condition over delusional disorder.
doctor.question: Have you seen things that other people could not see?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about visual hallucinations (seeing things others cannot see), but the provided symptom profile only covers delusions and functioning/duration, not hallucinations.

patient.answer:
No, I don’t think so. I mean… not in the sense of seeing a person standing there that nobody else can see, or objects moving, or anything like that.

Sometimes I notice things other people don’t seem to notice, but that’s more about paying attention, I think — like small details or patterns. But visually, like actually seeing something that isn’t there, no. I haven’t had that kind of experience.

There are times when I’ll double-check something, like if I think I saw a message notification or something out of the corner of my eye, but then it’s just the usual kind of mistake people make when they’re tired or distracted. Nothing where I’d say, “I saw something and everyone else says it wasn’t there.” So… no, I don’t think so.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has been a mood episode that could better explain the delusional belief, helping distinguish delusional disorder from schizophrenia or psychotic disorder due to another condition.
doctor.question: During the past year, have you had a period when your mood was unusually high or irritable?

target_item.reason: The question asks about periods of unusually high or irritable mood, which relates to manic or mood episodes; the provided symptom profile only covers delusions, duration, and functional impact, not mood elevation or irritability.

patient.answer:
Unusually high? No, I don’t think so. Not high like overly happy or energized in a way people would notice, if that’s what you mean.

I’ve definitely been irritable at times, but I think that’s been more in reaction to stress and arguments, not like a whole separate period where my mood changed and stayed that way for no reason. I can get frustrated, sure, especially when I feel like something isn’t being taken seriously, but I wouldn’t describe it as unusually irritable overall.

So… I guess my answer is no, not that I’ve noticed.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there are prominent negative symptoms, which would favor schizophrenia (F20) over persistent delusional disorder (F22) and help distinguish from organic delusional disorder (F06.2).
doctor.question: Over the past year, have you found that you care much less about things or have less motivation to do everyday activities than you used to?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: I still show up for my teaching sections, keep up with data analysis, ride my bike, and meet friends for chess; the main place this causes trouble is when my wife and I get stuck arguing about what her work schedule really means.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about reduced motivation or interest in everyday activities over the past year, which is most directly addressed by the profile indicating preserved functioning and usual activities apart from the marital impact of the delusion.

patient.answer:
No, not really. I mean, I wouldn’t say I’ve stopped caring about things in general or that I can’t get myself to do normal activities.

I still show up for my teaching sections, and I keep up with the data analysis I’m supposed to be doing. I ride my bike pretty regularly, too — not every single day, but enough that it’s still part of my routine. And I still meet friends for chess, which I wouldn’t do if I’d completely lost interest in things. I actually still enjoy that, especially because it’s structured, you know, there’s something clear to focus on.

The main place where things get disrupted is at home, when my wife and I get stuck arguing about her work schedule and what it really means. That can take over an evening, and then I might not feel like doing much afterward. But it’s not like I’ve lost motivation across the board. It’s more that this one situation keeps pulling energy and attention away from everything else.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has been prominent deterioration in overall functioning, which would favor schizophrenia over delusional disorder and help separate F20 from F22/F06.2.
doctor.question: Over the past year, has your ability to function at work or in your daily life gotten markedly worse?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: I still show up for my teaching sections, keep up with data analysis, ride my bike, and meet friends for chess; the main place this causes trouble is when my wife and I get stuck arguing about what her work schedule really means.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether overall work or daily functioning has become markedly worse, which directly matches the profile item about functioning not being markedly impaired except for the delusion's impact.

patient.answer:
Markedly worse? I don’t think I’d put it that strongly. I mean, I’m still functioning. I still show up for my teaching sections, and I’m not missing them or just disappearing or anything. I keep up with the data analysis I’m supposed to be doing, maybe not always with the same mental space I’d like, but it gets done.

And day-to-day, I still have routines. I ride my bike, I meet friends for chess, I do those things. So it’s not like my life has collapsed or I can’t manage basic responsibilities.

Where it does get worse — or where it causes the most trouble — is at home. My wife and I can get stuck arguing about her work schedule and what it really means, and then that can eat up a lot of time and energy. It can make the evening feel like it’s been taken over. So yes, it causes problems, but I wouldn’t say my overall ability to work or get through daily life has gotten markedly worse. It’s more contained than that, mostly around the arguments with her.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the delusional belief has bizarre/impossible content suggestive of schizophrenia rather than a non-bizarre delusional disorder or secondary psychosis.
doctor.question: Do you think your wife is communicating with you through secret codes hidden in ordinary work messages?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I know my wife says the late meetings and little changes in her work messages are just normal office stuff, but for the past year they’ve lined up too precisely to feel accidental, like there’s a private signal in them meant to tell me something she won’t say directly.
target_item.reason: The question directly asks about a fixed belief that the wife’s ordinary work messages contain hidden secret codes or signals, which matches the delusions profile.

patient.answer:
I wouldn’t put it exactly like “secret codes,” because that makes it sound… I don’t know, like something from a movie. But yes, I do think there are things in her work messages that mean more than she admits.

She’ll say it’s just normal office scheduling — a late meeting, a small change in wording, a time shifted by half an hour, some ordinary little phrase — but over the past year, those things have lined up too precisely to feel accidental. It’s not one message by itself. If it were one message, fine, I could ignore it. It’s the pattern. The timing, the way the wording changes, when the meetings appear, when they get moved. It feels like there’s a private signal in there, like she’s trying to communicate something indirectly instead of just saying it to me plainly.

And when I ask her, she says I’m reading too much into it, but that doesn’t really answer why it keeps happening in these exact ways. So… yes, I think there’s meaning hidden in ordinary work messages. I don’t know if I’d call it a code, but it feels intentional.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is an organic cause by assessing recent substance or medication exposure associated with delusions.
doctor.question: Before these beliefs started, did you begin using any drugs or start any new medication?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about substance or medication-induced causes before the beliefs began, but the provided symptom profile does not include drug use or new medication information.

patient.answer:
No, not that I can think of. I mean, I wasn’t suddenly using drugs or anything like that before this started, and I don’t remember starting some new medication around then.

I’m trying to think if there was anything even incidental — like a cold medicine or something I took once or twice — but nothing that stands out as a real change. My routine was basically the same. If you mean recreational drugs, no. And if you mean a prescription that began right before all this, I don’t think so.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there are persistent auditory hallucinations, which would strongly favor schizophrenia over delusional disorder and help separate a primary psychotic disorder from a non-schizophrenic delusional condition.
doctor.question: Have you ever heard your wife’s voice speaking to you when she was not actually there?

target_item.reason: The question is asking about auditory hallucinations, specifically hearing the wife’s voice when she is not present. The provided symptom profile covers delusions, functioning, impairment, and duration, but does not include hallucinations.

patient.answer:
No, I don’t think so. I mean, I’ve replayed conversations with her in my head, obviously — especially after an argument, where I can almost hear the tone she used or remember exactly how she said something — but that’s memory, not her actually speaking when she isn’t there.

I haven’t had a situation where I’m sitting alone and suddenly hear her voice talking to me from another room or anything like that. If I hear something, there’s usually a real explanation, like the TV, or someone outside, or just me thinking about what she said earlier. So no, not in the sense that you mean.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is a first-rank psychotic symptom of delusional perception/reference beyond the circumscribed marital belief, which would favor schizophrenia (F20) over persistent delusional disorder (F22) and organic delusional disorder (F06.2).
doctor.question: Have ordinary events or objects ever suddenly seemed to carry a special message meant specifically for you?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I know my wife says the late meetings and little changes in her work messages are just normal office stuff, but for the past year they’ve lined up too precisely to feel accidental, like there’s a private signal in them meant to tell me something she won’t say directly.
target_item.reason: The question asks about ordinary events or objects carrying special messages meant specifically for the patient, which directly relates to the fixed belief that his wife's ordinary work messages contain private signals or hidden meaning.

patient.answer:
Yes… I think that’s probably the closest way to describe it. Not every object or every little thing, but ordinary things like her work messages, meeting times, the wording she uses, small changes that other people would probably say are meaningless. To me they don’t feel random.

She’ll say a late meeting is just a late meeting, or that a phrase in a message is just how people at her office talk, or that a time shifting by half an hour doesn’t mean anything. And if it happened once, I’d agree. I’m not saying one calendar change proves anything. But over the past year, these things have lined up in a way that feels too precise. Like the timing and the wording are arranged to carry something extra.

It feels like there’s a message meant for me in it — not always clear, not like someone handing me a note and saying exactly what they mean — more like a private signal. Like she’s trying to tell me something indirectly, something she won’t just say out loud if I ask her. And when I do ask, she tells me I’m reading into it, but that doesn’t really make the pattern go away. So yes, ordinary things have seemed to carry a special meaning for me, especially with her work messages and those late meetings.

opening_question.intent: Learn the patient's main concern or reason for seeking psychiatric care today
opening_question.question: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient describes a persistent, systematized delusional belief for about one year that his wife's ordinary work messages and schedule changes contain hidden personal signals, with partial acknowledgment of possible error but clear conviction overall. Psychotic symptoms are otherwise circumscribed: no hallucinations, no thought control, no disorganized speech/behavior, no negative symptoms, no marked functional decline, and no mood episode explaining the belief. There is no evidence of a medical, neurological, substance-related, or medication-induced cause. This presentation is most consistent with delusional disorder.
